extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in moral philosophy and Montaigne's essays
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance personal essay reflecting on the morality, prudence, and motives of suicide, courage, curiosity, and conscience, illustrated with historical and literary examples. The text offers evaluative principles about when death may be justified, the nature of bravery and shame, and the inward effects of conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bravery vs fear of future ills
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fear of future ills often makes men run into extreme danger; he is truly brave who boldly dares withstand the mischiefs he apprehends, when they confront him and can be deferred.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate courage by a person's conduct when danger is present rather than by anticipatory fear; avoid being driven to rash acts by dread of what may come. Example: the gladiator who hopes on in the arena despite the crowd's signal for death. Anti-pattern: preemptive panic leading to precipitous decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against contempt of one's own life
rubrics_metrics.description: It is against nature for us to contemn and make little account of ourselves; ‘tis a disease particular to man, and not discerned in any other creatures, to hate and despise itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life is our being and all we have; to undervalue it is a vice. The desire to be something other than what one is (e.g., to be an angel) is vain because it confers no actual benefit. Use this criterion to criticize voluntary self-contempt and self-destruction motivated by contempt rather than necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death offers no real security or advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Security, indolence, impassability, the privation of the evils of this life, which we pretend to purchase at the price of dying, are of no manner of advantage to us: that man evades war to very little purpose who can have no fruition of peace; and as little to the purpose does he avoid trouble who cannot enjoy repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count death as a means to secure future enjoyment or peace — death prevents enjoyment just as much as it prevents suffering. Use this to judge attempts to 'buy' security by ending life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits for justifying self-murder ('reasonable exit')
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been great debate what occasions are sufficient to justify the meditation of self-murder, which they call 'A reasonable exit.' ... they say that men must often die for trivial causes, seeing those that detain us in life are of no very great weight, yet there is to be some limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a distinction between rash, trivial motives for suicide and grave, limiting occasions that might justify it (authors debate where that line lies). Historical authorities (Pliny, Seneca) propose narrow exceptional cases (e.g., prolonged disabling disease) as potentially excusable; consider severity, duration, and loss of faculties when judging justification. Anti-pattern: treating every private misery as sufficient ground for self-destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass or fanatic suicide as irrational social contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: There are fantastic and senseless humours that have prompted not only individual men, but whole nations to destroy themselves... what arguments and persuasion cannot do with individual men, they can do with all, the ardour of society ravishing particular judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating collective acts of self-destruction, account for social contagion and the diminished individual judgment in crowds; treat such universal resolutions as fiercer in appearance but often less rational than solitary, considered acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide to avoid dishonor, slavery, or rape can be seen as honourable
rubrics_metrics.description: The good man Razis... choosing rather to die nobly than to fall into the hands of his wicked adversaries and suffer himself to be cruelly butchered... The Sicilian father killed his daughters and then himself to deliver them from slavery and dishonour. Ecclesiastical examples (Pelagia, Sophronia) embraced death to secure from outrages against religion and honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a tradition that self-destruction to avoid abasement, slavery, or sexual violence may be considered an honourable response in some moral frameworks. Use historical examples to justify this evaluation, but weigh alternatives and context carefully (e.g., possibility of resistance, deliverance, or survival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain and fear of a worse death as excusable motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Pain and the fear of a worse death seem to me the most excusable incitements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sympathetic evaluation of suicide prompted by unbearable pain or a prospect of something worse; distinguish these cases from suicides based on petty motives. Example: Pliny's list of diseases considered grounds for self-killing (e.g., suppressed urine from bladder stone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide from hope of a better life (religious motive) is not always despair
rubrics_metrics.description: By which it appears how improperly we call this voluntary dissolution, despair, to which the eagerness of hope often inclines us... St. Paul: 'I desire to be with Christ.' Cleombrotus, having read Plato’s Phaedo, threw himself into the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish suicides driven by yearning for an afterlife or spiritual consummation from suicides driven by despair; such acts may stem from 'calm and temperate desire' following deliberate judgment. Evaluate motive and mental state rather than assume uniform culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: State regulation and socially-sanctioned voluntary death
rubrics_metrics.description: There was kept in our city of Marseilles a poison prepared out of hemlock, at the public charge, for those who had a mind to hasten their end, having first, before the six hundred, who were their senate, given account of the reasons and motives of their design, and it was not otherwise lawful, than by leave from the magistrate and upon just occasion to do violence to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some polities historically regulated voluntary death by requiring official approval; when assessing the permissibility of suicide, consider legal and communal frameworks that condition or permit it. Use as a criterion for legitimacy in a civic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence regarding curiosity and opening letters
rubrics_metrics.description: I never open any letters directed to another... Never was man less inquisitive or less prying into other men’s affairs than I... A wise man may, I think, out of respect to another, as not to disturb the company, as Rusticus did, or not to break off another affair of importance in hand, defer to read or hear any new thing that is brought him; but for his own interest or particular pleasure, especially if he be a public minister, that he will not interrupt his dinner or break his sleep is inexcusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance courtesy (deferring to avoid disturbing others) with public duty and self-interest. As a rule: do not open letters meant for others; do not let courtesy excuse neglect of pressing responsibilities. Historical anecdotes (Caesar, Archias) illustrate pitfalls of deferral. Anti-pattern: excessive negligence that endangers public office or personal safety by ignoring urgent messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for other people's privacy (avoid prying)
rubrics_metrics.description: I never open any letters directed to another; not only those intrusted with me, but even such as fortune has guided to my hand; and am angry with myself if my eyes unawares steal any contents of letters of importance he is reading when I stand near a great man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the privacy of others' correspondence as a moral rule; prying is improper even when temptation arises. Use this as an interpersonal ethical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as internal judge and punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: It makes us betray, accuse, and fight against ourselves... Whoever expects punishment already suffers it... Wickedness contrives torments against itself... 'Tis the first punishment of sin that no man absolves himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an agent's inner state (guilt, self-accusation, nightmares, torments) as evidence of moral culpability and as a form of punishment independent of external sanction. Examples: Bessus confessing parricide; dream-images revealing guilt. Anti-pattern: assuming external punishment is the only moral consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conscience confers bravery and assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: As an ill conscience fills us with fear, so a good one gives us greater confidence and assurance; and I can truly say that I have gone through several hazards with a more steady pace in consideration of the secret knowledge I had of my own will and the innocence of my intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging conduct under trial or danger, give weight to the steadiness that comes from innocence of intention. Historical examples (Scipio's comportment before accusations) illustrate how a clear conscience manifests in composure and moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torture is an unreliable test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The putting men to the rack is a dangerous invention... for why should pain sooner make me confess what really is, than force me to say what is not? ... Pain will make even the innocent lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider confessions under extreme pain as unreliable; do not treat torture-induced statements as sound evidence. Use awareness of the effects of suffering on testimony when evaluating claims obtained under duress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual violence against women is a grave affront and often justifies extreme avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Of violences offered to the conscience, that against the chastity of woman is, in my opinion, most to be avoided, forasmuch as there is a certain pleasure naturally mixed with it, and for that reason the dissent therein cannot be sufficiently perfect and entire...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat threats to female chastity as particularly severe violations of conscience that may morally justify extreme actions (including self-sacrifice) to avoid rape or dishonor. Use historical and hagiographic examples (Pelagia, Sophronia) as precedent, but assess case specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnanimous death by combat has moral weight distinct from passive suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: The death of the bishop, sword in hand, has more of magnanimity in it, and less of sentiment, the ardour of combat taking away part of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish deaths chosen in active, combative, or sacrificial contexts (which show courage and public-mindedness) from passive suicides motivated by private sentiment. When evaluating the nobility of a death, consider whether it served a public or martial purpose.
